Messages.Author: librarian
Messages.Body:
My feeling is that almost all the time, flicking a bleed is better than
merely reducing it. I was wondering if people would like to expand on
times when that is wrong.

If you don't have access to flick, but do have access to reduce,
obviously reduce is better than nothing (Serpentis, Potence, etc).

But if you can do either (AUS), then why not flick instead of reduce?
witness1 (John Newquist) posted back in January that counter is good if
you are going to suffer multiple bleeds of relatively small size (1-3),
since TC doesn't tap you, while TM/My Enemy's Enemy/etc does. Is that
the only time when Telepathic Counter is better than TM?

Oh wait, if you are playing a deck like Robert Scythe's Bartholemew deck
(if he's untapped at the beginning of your turn, gain a pool. He Tele
Counters and Folderols bleeds).

I guess the only other time might be when you don't have a lot of blood
on vamps and paying for TM is a challenge. Even then, MyEnemy's Enemy
seems like a better bet...

I never play with Tele Counter, always opting for Tele Misdirection, esp
because it also doubles as intercept. I won't even sprinkle in Tele
Counter.

But I'm willing to listen to reason and ranting to show me why I'm wrong...

Thanks,

chris

Messages.Author: Juggernaut1981
Messages.Body:


One of the most convincing uses I find for Reduce as a tactic is to
cause frustration to your predator, but also it helps you in some
cross table situations.

My preferred tactic for reduce is to frustrate my predator in three
main ways:
#1 Handjam: S&B decks HATE choking on stealth... so don't block and
reduce instead. Same goes for "Bleed'n'Smash"... let them die on
handjam.
#2 They flick at you: Reducing flicks at you keep you and your x-table
on good terms and also means that your predator has done very little
to change your table-state (you can still block, potentially reduce
their actions, haven't gotten into a combat with Hektor x-table)
#3 Contempt: you aren't blocking their actions, you aren't really
doing anything to them... you don't care that they are bleeding you...
(insert acting to emphasise your thinly veiled contempt at their
feeble attacks on you) while you turn around and do your best to
brutally savage your prey. Sure it's a "playing the man" tactic, but
in VTES that's all part of the mix.

The changes to the way reduce functions with bleeds has pulled back
another tactic I would use in an AUS flick-reduce deck. Previously
bleeds were reduced against you and not so against your prey, bleed-
amounts appeared to reset when you changed target. So I would block
and generate some light intercept, then reduce it to suck out any
bleed modifiers, then "fail to block" and flick it. My prey has
watched me struggling hard to block/reduce something (giving the
impression to both Prey & Pred I don't have a flick) and then flick it
at them with stealth and +bleed on it.

Messages.Author: brandons...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:


Reasons why reduce is *sometimes* better than bounce (a few, scattered
examples, some of which you have mentioned)
1) Inaccessability of AUS or dom with the desired crypt
2) May not want to hurt prey before your turn (i.e. Parity Shift,
Personal Involvement)
3) Bounce usually taps the bouncer, where reduction does not (compare
an untapped AUS minion fighting a bunch of bleeds of 1-2 vs the same
minion trying to bounce all of those bleeds. Bounce. Wake + Bounce.
Wake + Bounce (5 cards) vs TC, TC, TC (3 cards, free)
4) Sometimes there are efficiency issues, usually working against
reduction, sometimes not (see #3). Depends on the meta.
5) Specific cards' benefits:
- Confusion of the eye as reduction/vote hosing
-Wrong and Crosswise as reduction/ vote hosing
-Ecstacy as helping you tempt minions at SER
Note- the first two cards can easily be combined with Malk/!Malk. If
you want a pure dem/DEM deck, Wrong and Crosswise is really good.
6) Perverse satisfaction with playing funky cards (I'm looking at you,
Raille)

Just a few ideas to mull over.... There are obviously good reasons for
not using reduce, but the above are a few reasons for using it.

Brandon

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
librarian wrote:
> My feeling is that almost all the time, flicking a bleed is better than
> merely reducing it. I was wondering if people would like to expand on
> times when that is wrong.

You mention: no access to bounce, staying untapped to handle multiple small
bleeds, and blood management.

To that, add:

Reduction lets you keep the Edge.

If your prey has bounce and her prey does not, reduce may be better than letting
your prey further weaken her prey.

Likewise, if you're not a bleed deck yourself, bouncing bleed may help your prey
"cycle" bounce out of her hand (and draw into the intercept she needs to block
your referendums).

Bounce can be bounced back to you, leaving you to pay the whole bleed.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Feb 23, 6:57 pm, librarian <aucti...@superfuncards.com> wrote:
> My feeling is that almost all the time, flicking a bleed is better than
> merely reducing it.  I was wondering if people would like to expand on
> times when that is wrong.

Most of the time, bounce is just better. I mean, yeah, once and a
while, it goes badly, but for the most part, bounce is just so
stupidly powerful and effective than bleed reduction, if you have
bounce available, is just not a great idea.

The trick is when you don't have bounce available--I really like non
Auspex based bounce, and am on record many times that I'd like to see
more *good* non Auspex based bleed reduction (i.e. cards that are,
like, do something useful at inferior and reduce a bleed by 2 at
superior like the super obvious example of "obf: +1 stealth. OBF:
Reduce a bleed by 2.") The game has slowly and klunkily been moving in
that direction, but I think that most of the non Auspex bleed
reduction cards are kind of janky. Truth in Ink is totally reasonable
(although it lacks flexibility) and I use it all the time; Nest of
Eagles is totally good in moderation for the Assamites. I like Friend
of Mine in Anarch decks (although it totally could have been free and
still not remotely too good) while I find the free Detect Authority
seems less attractive, as Tha usually comes with Dom or Aus anyway.

I got a lot of mileage out of Auspex reduction in a weenie aus/obf
deck that mostly revolved around Victoria and keeping the edge (which
Reduction is more successful at than bounce), which worked ok, but
really, bounce would have probably been just all around better. Which
is usually the case.

> If you don't have access to flick, but do have access to reduce,
> obviously reduce is better than nothing (Serpentis, Potence, etc).

Exactly. Which is why I'd like to see it show up more. Steadfastness
is ok, but only reduces by 1 (which isn't generally worth it, even on
a flexible card). Make cards like that that reduce by 2 at superior.

> But if you can do either (AUS), then why not flick instead of reduce?
> witness1 (John Newquist) posted back in January that counter is good if
> you are going to suffer multiple bleeds of relatively small size (1-3),
> since TC doesn't tap you, while TM/My Enemy's Enemy/etc does.  Is that
> the only time when Telepathic Counter is better than TM?

Yeah, there was a lot of analysis of this in that thread, and John's
situation was a solid one (having bounce and reduction in a single
deck is good, as you can reduce the first bleed and then bounce the
second on 2 cards, where trying to bounce both bleeds takes 3 due to
being tapped the first time, assuming AUS bounce), but for my money, I
generally prefer the certainty of one or the other instead of both.
But that is me.

> I never play with Tele Counter, always opting for Tele Misdirection, esp
> because it also doubles as intercept.  I won't even sprinkle in Tele
> Counter.

I'm in the same boat.

> But I'm willing to listen to reason and ranting to show me why I'm wrong...

I generally don't think you are. Again, if you have no bounce
available? I like reduction, and would like to see more of it where no
bounce is available. But if you have dom or AUS? Bounce is going to
take up the card slots the vast majority of the time.

-Peter

Messages.Author: chfa...@hotmail.com
Messages.Body:
A clever prey will work together with your predator to slow you down.
A clever predator will work together with your prey to avoid you from
getting your VP.
An additional reason for not playing flicks/bounces is to avoid your
prey from cycling his hand on your predator's bleed.

There's also another reason, an extension of something already
addressed by brandon on his response (see topic 3 of his message)

IMHO, every decision you make to include a card on a deck means
leaving out something else that may help you oust your prey and
ultimately win the game.

Having to create those extra slots to house your flicks will mean you
may have to weaken your main deck strategy.

Regards,

Claudio Gomes

yet... you can't bounce when there is only 2 people left in the game

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Feb 24, 7:57 am, klaita...@gmail.com wrote:
> You can also easily craft in rather effective reduce module. Just play
> Isabel de Leon (or any other 3 cap with AUS) and a handful of
> telepathic counters, you probably wont slow your forward action much
> by just leaving her untapped every turn to reduce bleeds.

Sure, but this falls back on the concept of if you are going to have
Isabel de Leon and a handful of Telepathic Counters, why not have
Isabel de Leon and a handful of Telepathic Misdirections? A handful
implies not a ton (6-8?), which means you are unlikely to have
multiples in hand at any given time. At which point, bounce is
generally a much better option (if you have 1 bleed defense card, you
are usually better with the bounce than you are the reduction). That,
and the flexibility of it also being +1 intercept (in case your
predator doesn't bleed you) makes it even stronger.

Yeah, if you have Isabel de Leon standing around, and, like, 15
Telepathic Counters, that is going to be pretty solid bleed defense.
But then having 15 Telepathic Counters in your deck comes with all
sorts of other problems.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
On Feb 23, 3:57 pm, librarian <aucti...@superfuncards.com> wrote:
> My feeling is that almost all the time, flicking a bleed is better than
> merely reducing it.  I was wondering if people would like to expand on
> times when that is wrong.
>

> But I'm willing to listen to reason and ranting to show me why I'm wrong...

I see reduce as a mindgame. There are various ways it's situationally
better, like how a deck is probably going to run out of wakes, jamming
a prey on bleed defense, jamming a combat predator on combat, etc.
But, the mystery benefit is how much it disguises your deck, throws
off your opponents, or whatever.

For instance, it's more passive than bounce. For me, since I lowball
offense all of the time, it's too passive as I need bounce to generate
a reasonable amount of pool damage. But, it's an interesting
distraction to a deck with Govern/Conditioning, Legal/Aire, or
whatever. Does it convey false weakness? A more esoteric plan for
winning?

It's more friendly. Sure grandpredator, bleed like crazy, I can suck
it up. It may be more of a comfort to a grandpredator than bounce
wars, especially as bounce wars can lead to overloading someone's
wakes. And, while reduce looks better in an endgame for you, may very
well want someone else to be playing it in a threesome rather than
engage in bounce wars. Does this gain much, if anything? Depends
upon how much you can position yourself at a table and how much doing
so buys you something.

How do people's perceptions of decks change when someone just
reduces? This is what I see being the key to justifying reduction.
Otherwise, yeah, bounce is so powerful against the typical field that
it's hard to stray from (or not bolt on).

On Feb 24, 5:23 pm, James Coupe <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:
> Taken in isolation, the tapping and the blood cost.

Well, yes, but the context was a "bleed defense module" that consisted
of Isabel de Leon and a handful of Telepathic Counters. Assuming a
"handful" means "not so many that you'll regularly have multiples in
hand", the blood cost and the tapping is going to be mostly
irrelevant, as Isabel's whole purpose is just standing around and
protecting you from bleeds. If she can reduce a single bleed by 2 or
bounce a single bleed of X, most of the time, she is going to be
better off used to bounce a bleed of X instead of just reducing the
bleed by 2 (assuming you are being bled for significant amounts; if
you are only being bled for 1 at a time, the Telepathic Counters are
going to be better, but if you are only ever being bled for 1 at a
time, you probably have other significant things to worry about).

Even if she never hunts and only bounces a single bleed of 3 a turn,
those 3 bounced bleeds are going to pay for Isabel 3 times.

Again, as I mentioned in my previous post, if you are going to have a
lot of Telepathic Counters, and are being bled for middle amounts a
lot, and she can reduce multiple bleeds a turn, then the Counters are
going to be gold. But that it s lot of "and"s in there. And most of
the time, the bounce is just going to be better.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Juggernaut1981

On Feb 25, 9:23 am, James Coupe <ja...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:


As mentioned by myself and others, the major reasons for using reduce
are:

#1 Mindgames...
#2 Usability in the final game stages
#3 Breaking the Flick Chain

The two can combine very effectively when you have a bleed-heavy
predator in the final game stages. If he knows that he is not going
to really get anywhere by tapping out to bleed it may convince them to
go into a bloating tactic to try outlast the remaining one or two
players (including yourself).

Building up frustration in your predator can be a very very effective
game tactic. It subtly encourages them to make mistakes, to leave
themselves open, to over or under-estimate their effectiveness and so
on. Sure more experienced players are harder to frustrate like this,
but it can demoralise your predator when you reduce a full-on bleed
assault with one or two minions with AUS...

They are also gold if you have Archon Investigations in the deck. You
can tempt a predator to overstep the mark and try get you for 4 or
more before you reduce...

Flick-chains are a common enough thing on a table with a lot of AUS
and DOM. You can see a bleed get passed all the way around a table
(2006 Qualifiers in Sydney saw two vampires get Archon
Investigation'ed by the Predator Methuselah after being passed around
a table in the one game... total of 7 Archon Investigations played
during that qualifier of about 20 players). By using reduce, you can
control which bleeds get passed around and limit some of the pressure
applied to a X-table buddy. It may mean that he only has to deal with
1 or 2 players worth of bleeds rather than 4 players worth of bleeds.

Messages.Author: opao...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
i think the problem lies in how we are conceiving this argument.
Bounce (aka Flick) IS reduction. it just functions differently. it
reduces 100% (though not permanently upon the bleed) + adds offense,
for the price of a tapped minion, card, and blood. other forms of
reduction reduce by fixed number (permanently) for the price of a
played card (and occasionally a blood). naturally one plays up better
versus swarms and other extenuating situations -- the advantage is
fixed in the cost of not having to tap a minion and not having to
worry about the bleed coming back full force (bounced back). but
overall that just lengthens an already usually long game, plays jedi
mind tricks which may or may not work, and shoots for a smaller slice
of the threatening bleed pie.

when i went through some silly sphere of influence thinking, with
circles representing areas of interaction, i found that intercept and
stealth is pretty much it's own specialized game, its Action Sphere if
you will. however this sphere affects everything from gear, votes,
combat, and bleed. so that's why i don't really accept the argument
that intercept exists as a solution to complaints about bleed's
current status, because technically it can be a solution to all minion
actions. it affects all minion action spheres up until the point it
fails. however combat and votes do have quite a pool of cards to
interact and contest once the intercept sphere has been breached,
being their Combat and Vote Sphere respectively.

but bleed, fixed reduce, AI-esque reduction + punishment, and bounce
is its own sphere, the Bleed Sphere. and in that sphere the pool of
cards is very limited indeed in comparison. there is less room for
contestation of the most basic function of the game than there is of
the more highly specialized functions! O_o further, the exercise we
are doing now also highlights the strengths and weaknesses of the two
most powerful and prevalent archetypes of contestation defense within
this Bleed Sphere. but note, outside of endgame, swarms, and
specialized circumstances, bounce tends to find itself as the better
general tool for bleed contestation in the Bleed Sphere. additionally
it re-sets up the Action Sphere for its own offensive uses -- an epic
benefit with few decent caliber responses by the acting player (which
is for the best in this game currently). bleed contestation could
definitely use a new look for creative solutions. perhaps focus on
percentage reduction or new offense/defense rewards and penalties
could be added to spice new reduction cards (because i've established
Bleed Sphere defenses are essentially all reducers). however we must
continually keep in mind how strong "100% reduction + offense" is in
this sphere, otherwise new solutions will fail as soon as they are
born.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Feb 25, 1:54 pm, opaop...@yahoo.com wrote:
> i think the problem lies in how we are conceiving this argument.
> Bounce (aka Flick) IS reduction. it just functions differently.

Well, kind of? Certainly in the context of this discussion,
"Reduction" is specifically referring to bleed reduction cards that
don't send the bleed somewhere else. So claiming that "Bounce" (i.e.
cards that move a bleed from one target to another) is
"Reduction" (i.e. cards that reduce the amount of a bleed a fixed
number but keeps the target of the bleed the same) is kind of oblique
semantic juggling. Yes, in effect, a bleed bounce cards reduces the
amount of bleeding that happens to you, but that isn't really what
anyone is talking about.

-Peter

There are very valid reasons for using Reduce not Flick/Bounce...
Personally I would almost never consider using Telepathic Misdirection
in a !Salubri deck even though there is a giant pile of aus/AUS
amongst them. I would however use the Aversion at any of the
levels... [cel] is good (reduce for celerity and no Anarchiness??
woohoo!!), [val] is nice (no edge for you!! bye bye Snake-deck of
Enticement Doom), [VAL] is great (chew on that weenie bleeder)

Sure most !Salubri decks will treat your bleeding with a pile of block
and a lightsabre (Sword of the Righteous + Bastard Sword + other
Valeren goodies), but for those !Salubri that don't just block
everything around them and lightsabre you... Aversion is GOLD. No
need to tap on a bleed, you can pick on the hunting Vampire. No need
to worry about those snakes bleeding for 1 or 2... they can't
Enticement you afterwards cause they don't get the edge. No need to
worry about those "Embrace/Waters of the Duat/Tumnimos" breed like
rats and bleed for 1 with 10 minions... you just Aversion them at
[VAL] and block every attempt they make to remove the thing.

Flick is very effective at increasing the pressure on a prey who
cannot flick. If they can flick, all you're doing is piling up more
players worth of pressure on the guy without AUS or DOM who is at the
end of the Flick-Chain.

Here is where flick fails: it dumps more pressure in one location than
would normally be there and you can't necessarily control that
pressure. With Reduce I negate the pressure on me while I continue to
apply the same pressure to my prey.

Flick = pile up pressure somewhere
Reduce = reduce the pressure applied to you

> pressure.  With Reduce I negate the pressure on me while I continue to
> apply the same pressure to my prey.

Sure, but if you are being bled for 3-5 per action reliably, the
reduction is just going to slow down your death a bit, where if you
had bounce, it might just oust your prey instead.

Again, reduction is ok, and good when you have no other options (i.e.
you are Black Hand without bounce disciplines, or you are the
Assamites for example). And good in combination with some Bounce if
you have AUS. But for the most part, bounce is going to work better on
average.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
On Feb 25, 6:17 pm, Peter D Bakija <p...@lightlink.com> wrote:
>
> > Here is where flick fails: it dumps more pressure in one location than
> > would normally be there and you can't necessarily control that
> > pressure.  With Reduce I negate the pressure on me while I continue to
> > apply the same pressure to my prey.
>
> Sure, but if you are being bled for 3-5 per action reliably, the
> reduction is just going to slow down your death a bit, where if you
> had bounce, it might just oust your prey instead.
>

Here might be a meta-game issue. Around here, bleeds of 3+ at 1 or
more stealth are fairly uncommon. I mean, it happens - the newer
players have a dem/obf deck that will do that (but rarely more than 3
or 4 at a click) and a dom/obt deck that can bleed for lots at lots of
stealth, mostly because those are the types of deck to recommend to
newer players, because they can win and are easy to build. But to
have 1 of them at a table is not a given - even somewhat uncommon.

Because bounce is so easy of a defense (and because of AI), a lot of
players have been building decks that don't have to bleed for 3+ at 1+
stealth to succeed. Swarm bleed (1 or 2 bleed at a time, more times
than you can bounce), block denial (one very nice one involve a
Francois Villon/Alexandra deck with Aching Beauty, Crocodile's Tongue,
Heart's Desire, Majesty, Change of Target, votes... etc..., and
another uses Nergal with Elder Intervention, Approximation of Loyalty,
and Psychomachia), bruise & bleed, and, of course, rush or voting.
Those decks that do intend to bleed for a lot tend to pack Spying
Mission and/or Revelations to sniff out bounce, and Two Wrongs is due
to become prevalent soon, since most in our playgroup have 2 of them.
Even for the heavy no-stealth bleeders, it's not a given that bounce
is better because you usually want to attempt to block before
bouncing, and that can be punished.

Bounce is certainly in use, but those decks that have access to AUS
and use reduction do not seem to be at a disadvantage. Bleed
reduction does have its advantages when compared with bounce, many of
which have been named in this thread - less cycling, edge doesn't
move, no chance for your grandprey to take the damage, more useful in
endgame (both because it's useful in 2-player, and because it can
facilitate withdrawal), generally less blood cost and no tapping,
etc... Plus there are cards like Folderol and Ignis Fatuus that can
be useful cross-table. In addition, spending 1 blood and possibly
tapping to send a blood to your prey at 0 stealth is unlikely to help
all that much, especially if rendered completely worthless by a Change
of Target. Reduction might do something as good as denying a Forced
March, Truth of 1000 Lies, or Freak Drive (inf) even in the case where
bounce *would* have given a success

Granted, if you compare any reduction card currently in print versus
Deflection, you will always come up lacking. Deflection is the
supreme bleed defense card, even taking into account the circumstances
listed above. But with most bleeds coming in at 2 or 3 bleed and 1 or
less stealth, and with Telepathic Misdirection costing a blood and
tapping, I don't think it's clear-cut which is better. If you have
access to Deflection, you pretty much have to use it. But if you have
AUS, I contend that a reduction-based defense can be just as good as a
bounce-based defense. In that case, I feel it depends on the metagame
and how much blood/pool-gain and untap you have. If you don't have
access to bounce (other than perhaps Lost in Translation), and do have
access to decent reduction (Truth in Ink, Aversion, Nest of Eagles,
and in some situations Ecstasy and Folderol and a few other cards with
multiple uses like Covincraft), then the decision is kind of made for
you, but I don't think it's that much of a handicap.

If the point is to hopefully beef up reduce, then I can't really
disagree, but if the point is that reduction is pointless when you can
graft on some bounce - I think that in some ways the game has moved
past that point, and at worst it's metagame dependent...

Messages.Author: XZealot
Messages.Body:
On Feb 23, 5:57 pm, librarian <aucti...@superfuncards.com> wrote:
> My feeling is that almost all the time, flicking a bleed is better than

> merely reducing it.  I was wondering if people would like to expand on
> times when that is wrong.

The advantange of flic versus reduction has to do with the average
size of the bleeds that you see.

If your average size of bleeds is less than 3 then Reduction is
superior

If your average size of bleeds is greater than 3 then Bounce is
superior

If your average size of bleeds is equal to 3 than there is no trade-
off

Under this model Reduction is the ability to reduce a bleed by 2 or
more, and Bounce is the ability to chose the new target of the bleed.

So sub-optimal cards tend to fall out of the model, such as Ecstasy,
My Enemy's Enemy, etc.

Oh, sure. I don't see bleeds of 5 at +3 stealth every game or

reliably (especially in a blind competition), and as they tend to be
incredibly debilitating when they do, you kind of *need* to plan for
them as the worst case scenario, which is why bounce tends to win the
card slot war; not 'cause you *know* you are going to run into huge
stealthy bleeds, but 'cause you might, and if you do, you are going to
die if you don't have the bounce, and the bounce is still gonna be
good against 2 point bleeds if that is all that is coming at you
anyway.

If you are talking about a local environment, and you can reliably
plan on only ever getting bled for 2 at a time for whatever reason,
then yeah, reduction could be pure gold. But if you are looking at
kind of a generic blind environment (like a tournament), I think big
bleeds at stealth are common enough to justify the bounce over the
reduction most of the time.

I'd never say it was pointless, but still, most of the time, in most

Messages.Author: Juggernaut1981
Messages.Body:
Everyone agrees that in any deck with [dom] or [DOM] as a major
feature... Redirection/Deflection is the pants. Since Dominate
doesn't really have a reduce card... we can assume that anyone who has
[dom] or [DOM] throughout their deck will be teflon-suiting that bleed
to their prey, like clockwork.

Let's assume that in most cases we are going to be talking about
Reduce in one of two contexts: Auspex or Bloodline Disciplines (Myt,
Val, Obe, Mel, etc).

Bloodline Disciplines:
#1 Most of these cards are more versatile and more powerful than
Telepathic Misdirection for comparable blood cost and often without a
tap.
#2 Most of the bloodline Disciplines come with either [dom] or [aus]
as a clan discipline (Myt, Val, Obe) or more combat disciplines (Val,
Vic, San)

Auspex-centred Decks are often wall/block decks of some kind. Either
the combat-wall (Tzimisce, Tor-Guns, Massasi hates everyone) or an
overt forward pressure + wall (Vote-Wall, Bleed-Wall, Attrition Wall
like Anarch Revolt/Smiling Jack decks)

A BLOCK DECK STRATEGY
Even if I am the super-freaky untap beast (read: big untap/act as if
untapped function in the deck) with a highly reliable 3+ Intercept...
there are still reasons why I would use a Telepathic Counter over a
Telepathic Misdirection. These hinge around me being able to more
effectively block actions.

#1 I know my predator/prey will want to perform an undirected action
that will be crucial to their turn (i.e. Hunt with a Superstar, Rescue
that Prince from torpor, remove the Anarch Revolt, etc)... if I reduce
their bleeds I can block more of their actions that protect
themselves. This can potentially force them to take fewer forward
actions (by losing minions to torpor or needing to hunt) or to really
put it all on the line to get me (leaving themselves vulnerable to
being bled heavily).

#2 Most decks that are going to want to bleed for 3+ will do so at
some level of stealth... bare minimum 1 from something like a Marijava
Ghoul or a Veil the Legions at Superior. No block = no cycling on
stealth... sure it may mean that they get a few more of those
undirected actions off as they burn through a handful of stealth, but
if they are a bleed deck then they'll choke slowly on their stealth or
spend it where they don't want to.

#3 Most decks that don't bleed for bucketloads at high stealth will
need to take undirected actions to breed. They will Enchant Kindred @
PRE, GtU @ DOM, Founders of the Ebony Kingdom and Breed actions
(Tumnimos/Waters of the Duat/The Embrace/etc)... these are the things
you want to block, not the trifling bleed for 1 from a small minion.
As either the Prey or Predator of these sorts of decks, having the
option to block either a bleed on myself or the Breed action, blocking
the Breed action will probably have greater long-term effect on the
game.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Feb 26, 2:13 am, "Kevin M." <youw...@imaspammer.org> wrote:
> Bleeds of 1 at 0 stealth are more common than all other types of bleed at
> any level of stealth put together.  So, does that mean that Reduce is a
> better option than we have previously considered?

Probably not for the reason I brought up before--I agree that bleeds
of 1 at 0 stealth are the most common bleed you see. But they also
aren't (generally speaking) the bleeds that oust you quickly. They
aren't the worst case scenario that blows you out of the game in 3
turns. The bleeds of 5 at +3 stealth are. Bleeds of 1 at 0 stealth are
something that, most of the time, decks can deal with without having
bounce. Again, if you are being bled for 1 at 0 stealth, you probably
have other things to worry about (like the Rushes that come with them,
or the Con Boons and 20 minions being made, or whatever), but as a
generic threat, you are generally better off ignoring the bleeds of 1
at 0 stealth (or blocking them or bloating to counteract them) than
you are building in specific bleed defense to deal with them.

The bleeds of 5 at +3 stealth, however, have the impact factor that
results in you dying very quickly; usually you take 3 bleeds of 5?
Your game is over. You take 3 bleeds of 1? You might not even notice
if you have some Blood Dolls in play. That is one of the *huge*
advantages bounce has over reduction and why it is so attractive; it
saves you from the worst case scenario and still is worth using in the
best case scenario. Reduction helps you in the best case scenario, but
doesn't actually help the worst case scenario that much.

-Peter

My point about Aversion is this...
Aversion at [VAL] ensures that your predator, if they bleed, will take
actions to remove the Aversion instead of leaving it there to weaken
their strategy. Aversions also Stack. So you can pile 2 or 3
Aversions onto the one vampire for the bleed of 3 at mild stealth
thereby reducing the bleed capacity of that minion to basically squat
all.

Now that you have slowed that minion to a crawl, they will want to
take actions to remove it (also removing the need to block bleeds from
those minions and buying you time to bloat or get your prey) and
blocking THOSE actions puts further slowdown on your predator (who
will be wanting to get rid of the Aversions before they accumulate all
over their vampires which he may continue to bleed with). Aversion
can be tactically used to put a significant slow-down on your predator
beyond the mere "reduce bleed" because they are convinced to take non-
bleed actions against you. This is similar to the tactics used with
Smiling Jack/Anarch Revolt wall decks that grind down prey pool and
then the minions by blocking attempts to remove the Jacks/Revolts.

That's also why I went into a longer discussion about AUS reduce
(since realistically the only debate to be had is whether AUS-Flick is
better than AUS-Reduce... because there is no reduce for DOM and DOM-
Flick is the pants...). My opinion is "No", the price of tapping to
far greater than the general and unspecific advantage or potentially
passing a big bleed onto your prey.

If you're worried, and regularly get worried, by bleeds of 4+ at 3+
stealth... then ditch 4 Wakes and stick in 4 Archon Investigations.
That will slow up the "supercheese" bleeding really fast decks if they
have a 50-50 bet you're packing an AI.

Sydney appears to have gone into a protracted phase of combat-oust,
vote-oust and "bleed for 3 or less at moderate sustainable stealth"
ever since the 2007 Qualifier where over 7 Archon Investigations were
played in 2 rounds amongst 20 players... including 5 in one game.
When you watch your bleed get flicked around to your predator and then
Archoned... it shows you that big bleeds at stealth is not only
dangerous to you, but also unlikely to hit your target. If you're
going to bleed big at stealth, you need to develop ways to control the
results or you'll give VPs away all over the table.

5+ bleeds at 3+ stealth = loose cannon that nobody wants on the table
because nobody needs to get that flicked at them at any time during
the game.

DOM-Flick = THE PANTS
AUS-Reduce = always reliable slowdown/defensive
AUS-Flick = not always worth the risk, not always reliable, no
guarantees on result
